learn.b: Every Go program lives in a package. A runnable program uses package main and has a function called main, which is where Go starts. The fmt package prints text to the screen.

The import line brings in other packages so you can use them. If you import a package and never use it, Go refuses to compile. Names that start with a capital letter, like Println, are exported, which means other packages can use them.

Println prints its arguments with a space between them and a newline at the end. Print does not add a newline. Printf uses a format string with verbs: %d for integers, %s for strings and %v for any value.
learn.code:
fmt.Println("Go", 1+2)
fmt.Printf("%d items\n", 3)

learn.b: Save the file as hello.go and run go run hello.go to compile and run it in one step. Use go build to make an executable file. Comments start with // for one line, or sit between /* and */.

learn.b: Use var to declare a variable, with a type after the name. A variable you declare without a value gets a zero value: 0 for numbers, an empty string for strings and false for booleans. You can also give a value right away.
learn.code:
var age int = 16
var name string
var ok bool
fmt.Println(age, name, ok)

learn.b: Inside a function you can write name := value and Go works out the type for you. The := form only works inside functions, not at the top of a file. Go also complains if a local variable is declared but never used.
learn.code:
score := 10
price := 2.5
greeting := "hi"

learn.b: The main types are int for whole numbers, float64 for decimals, string for text and bool for true or false. Go never mixes number types silently, so you convert by hand with the type name. Use const for values that never change.
learn.code:
x := 7
y := 2.0
fmt.Println(float64(x) / y)
const Pi = 3.14

learn.b: You can declare many variables on one line. Use var a, b = 1, 2 or a, b := 1, 2. You can also group them in a var block. Assigning later uses a plain = sign.
learn.code:
a, b := 1, 2
a = 5
fmt.Println(a, b)

learn.b: An if in Go has no parentheses around the condition, but the braces are required. You can add a short statement before the condition, and the variable it creates lives only inside the if. Use else if and else for other branches.
Go has just one loop keyword: for. The classic form has an init, a condition and a step. If you keep only the condition it works like while, and for with nothing is an infinite loop.
break leaves the loop at once. continue skips to the next round. Both work in every kind of for loop, and an infinite for { } usually ends with a break.

switch compares a value against several cases. Go stops after the matching case, so you do not write break. A case can list several values, and default runs when nothing matches. A switch with no value acts like a clean if chain.

qs.q: Which keyword is Go's only loop?
qs.why: Go uses for for every kind of loop.

learn.b: A function starts with func, then the name, the parameters with their types, and the return type. When neighbouring parameters share a type you can write the type once. Use return to send a value back.
A Go function can return more than one value by listing the types in parentheses. The caller receives them with a comma list. If you do not need one, throw it away with the blank identifier _.
You can name the results so they act like variables, and a bare return sends them back. A parameter written as nums ...int accepts any number of ints and behaves like a slice inside.
defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function ends, which is handy for cleanup. Functions are also values: you can store one in a variable or pass it around.

learn.b: An array has a fixed length that is part of its type, so [3]int and [4]int are different types. Elements start at index 0. Arrays are rarely used directly because slices are more flexible.
learn.code:
var a [3]int
a[0] = 7
b := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
fmt.Println(a, b, len(b))

learn.b: A slice is a window onto an array that can grow. Write it without a size: []int{1, 2, 3}. The slice expression s[1:3] takes elements from index 1 up to but not including 3. len gives the number of elements and cap the room available.

append adds elements and returns a new slice, so you must keep the result: s = append(s, 4). make creates a slice with a given length filled with zero values. copy copies elements from one slice into another.
learn.code:
s := make([]int, 3)
s = append(s, 4)
fmt.Println(s)

learn.b: Slices that come from the same array share the same data, so changing one can change the other. To loop over a slice use range, which gives the index and the value. Use _ if you do not need one of them.

learn.b: A map stores key and value pairs. Its type is written map[KeyType]ValueType. Create one with a literal or with make, which gives you an empty map ready to use.
learn.code:
ages := map[string]int{"Ana": 20}
scores := make(map[string]int)

learn.b: Use m[key] to read and m[key] = value to set or update. The built-in len tells you how many keys there are, and delete removes a key. Reading a missing key does not crash, it gives the zero value.
learn.code:
scores["Bo"] = 7
fmt.Println(scores["Bo"])
delete(scores, "Bo")
fmt.Println(len(scores))

learn.b: Because a missing key gives zero, you cannot tell it apart from a stored zero. Ask for two values: the second is true only if the key exists. This is called the comma ok idiom.

Use for key, value := range m to go through a map. The order is random on purpose, so never rely on it. A map that was never created is nil, and writing to a nil map crashes the program, so always create it with make or a literal.

learn.b: A struct groups related fields into one type. Define it with type Name struct, then create values with a literal. Read and write fields with a dot. Go has no classes, structs and methods do the same job.
A method is a function with a receiver written before its name. With a value receiver the method gets a copy, so changes inside do not affect the original.
If a method must change the original struct, use a pointer receiver such as (p *Person). Go lets you call it directly on a normal variable and handles the pointer for you.

The & operator gives the address of a variable and * follows a pointer to its value. Pointers let functions change data they are given. By convention a function named NewPerson builds and returns a struct, since Go has no constructors.
learn.code:
x := 5
p := &x
*p = 9
fmt.Println(x)

learn.b: An interface is a list of method signatures. Any type that has all those methods automatically satisfies the interface. There is no implements keyword, which is why Go calls it implicit.
A variable or parameter of an interface type can hold any value whose type has the methods. This lets one function work with many types, like a slice of Shapes.
The type any (the same as interface{}) has no methods, so every value fits in it. To get the real value back, use a type assertion v, ok := x.(string). The ok tells you whether it worked.
learn.code:
var x any = "hi"
s, ok := x.(string)
fmt.Println(s, ok)

learn.b: A type switch checks the real type of an interface value in each case. The fmt package also looks for a String() string method: if your type has it, Println uses it to print your value.

learn.b: Go has no exceptions for normal problems. Functions that can fail return an extra value of type error. The error interface is just one method, Error() string. A nil error means success.
Create an error with errors.New or fmt.Errorf. The caller checks if err != nil right after the call and deals with it. This pattern appears everywhere in Go code.
fmt.Errorf with the %w verb wraps an error and adds context. errors.Is checks whether a specific error is anywhere in the chain, and errors.As pulls out a particular error type.

Any type with an Error() string method is an error, so you can make your own with extra fields. panic stops the program for truly unexpected bugs, and recover inside a deferred function can catch it. Normal failures should use error values.

learn.b: Put the keyword go before a function call and it runs at the same time as the rest of your code. This is a goroutine, a very cheap thread. When main returns the program ends, even if goroutines are still running.
learn.code:
go fmt.Println("in a goroutine")
time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond)

learn.b: To wait for goroutines without guessing a sleep time, use sync.WaitGroup. Call Add before starting, Done when each goroutine finishes and Wait to block until all are done.
learn.code:
var wg sync.WaitGroup
wg.Add(1)
go func() {
    defer wg.Done()
    fmt.Println("work")
}()
wg.Wait()

learn.b: A channel is a typed pipe between goroutines. ch <- v sends and <-ch receives. On an unbuffered channel a send waits until someone receives. A buffered channel such as make(chan int, 2) holds that many values before it blocks.
learn.code:
ch := make(chan string)
go func() { ch <- "ping" }()
fmt.Println(<-ch)

learn.b: The sender can close a channel, and for v := range ch reads until it is closed. select waits on several channel operations at once and picks one that is ready. When goroutines share a variable, protect it with sync.Mutex using Lock and Unlock.

qs.q: Which keyword starts a goroutine?
qs.why: go before a call runs it concurrently.

qs.q: An unbuffered channel send blocks until what happens?
qs.why: Unbuffered channels synchronize sender and receiver.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.code:

go func() { ch <- "ping" }()
fmt.Println(<-ch)
qs.why: The goroutine sends ping and main receives it.

qs.q: A Go program waits for all goroutines to finish before main returns.
qs.why: The program exits when main returns.
